climbing_route.label: Ridge crest from the col
climbing_route.notes: From the low col on the crest between Old Snowy Mountain and Ives Peak, follow the ridge crest or a line just south of it over a rounded intermediate high point toward Ives' northwest ridge. Snowfields commonly linger in the col well into July, so an ice axe is worth carrying for early/mid-season attempts on the traverse.

climbing_route.label: Notch and exposed ledge traverse
climbing_route.notes: At the base of the true summit block a boot path threads up scree toward a notch between two rock outcrops; above the notch is a short cliff band — downclimb slightly and traverse a narrow, exposed ledge to gain the upper south face.

climbing_route.label: Upper south face to summit
climbing_route.notes: Scramble roughly 40 ft to climber's right on loose blocky rock, then up easy terrain to the 7,920-ft summit.

climbing_route.label: South slabs and talus to the summit
climbing_route.notes: A scatter of cairned, well-worn boot paths rather than a trail: pick the path of least resistance up the broad south-facing slabs and talus on the peak's east/left side, switchbacking and scrambling to the 8,485-ft summit. Loose rock and rockfall potential on the final slopes, especially with parties above you; full sun and thunderstorm exposure on the open talus; no water past the Colchuck Lake outlet.

climbing_route.label: Benches and ledges to the col west of Clark Mountain
climbing_route.notes: From the 7,200 ft spur, a rising traverse across broad benches — often snow-covered well into summer — and easy ledges leads to the ~7,600 ft col west of Clark Mountain.

climbing_route.label: Upper Richardson Glacier traverse
climbing_route.notes: A rising traverse across the upper Richardson Glacier reaches Luahna's East Ridge. Real crevasse hazard — carry glacier travel gear; the glacier has been reported thinning/broken-up and less straightforward in recent years.

climbing_route.label: East Ridge to the summit
climbing_route.notes: Scramble the East Ridge west to the summit.

climbing_route.label: Variation: south/southeast ridge (avoids the glacier)
climbing_route.notes: Parties wanting to avoid the glacier crossing can stay on rock from the basin and scramble Luahna's south/southeast ridge directly; several sources describe this as the more reliable line in low-snow years.

climbing_route.label: Arrow-marked scramble behind the sub-summit
climbing_route.notes: The final roughly 1,000-1,100 vertical feet is an exposed scramble, not a trail. Intermittent and often faded red arrows painted on the rock mark the line, which loops right then left behind a lower sub-summit. Expect loose rock ('kitty litter' on slabs) — staying precisely on the arrow-marked line matters, as it gets noticeably dicier off-route.

climbing_route.label: Snowfield/talus shelf above the Sandalee Glacier
climbing_route.notes: The line crosses a snowfield/talus shelf above the Sandalee Glacier; carry an ice axe if snow still covers the talus or the glacier traverse, common into midsummer.

climbing_route.label: Summit shoulder
climbing_route.notes: A fairly level shoulder past an old radio installation leads to the true summit and former fire-lookout site. Real exposure on the ledges near the top.

climbing_route.label: Slabby rock above the lower cliff band
climbing_route.notes: Leaving the trail near Upper Eagle Lake, head northwest through larch stands toward a notch, staying right of the prominent rock wall above the lake, and scramble slabby rock to get above a lower cliff band.

climbing_route.label: Traverse left below the upper cliff band
climbing_route.notes: Traverse left below the next cliff band, then climb steep, loose scree/rock to just below the summit block.

climbing_route.label: Summit block finish
climbing_route.notes: The final summit block above the loose scree/rock.

climbing_route.label: Variation: west slopes from Horsehead Pass
climbing_route.notes: For the easier line, continue past Lower Eagle Lake up to Horsehead Pass and climb the peak's west slopes.

climbing_route.label: Northeast Ridge crest from Luna Pass
climbing_route.notes: Skirt the rock knob that towers ~100 ft over Luna Pass via a broad ledge on its northwest face to reach the surprisingly gentle Northeast Ridge crest, then follow the ridge's many short ups and downs toward Fury — including a ~25-ft rock step with a climbable vertical crack (Class 3).

climbing_route.label: Heather chute and traverse to the rocky rib
climbing_route.notes: Where the ridge crest drops away, descend a steep, narrow heather chute (~500 ft) into a talus basin around 6,500 ft, then contour southwest across talus, heather, and polished slabs to a rocky rib that blocks easy passage. The lower of two ledge options — exposed scrambling on wet, mossy rock and steep heather — is generally preferred to the looser, more exposed upper ledge.

climbing_route.label: Southeast Glacier
climbing_route.notes: Beyond the rib, rope up for the crevassed Southeast Glacier (starting ~6,500-7,000 ft): ascend its true right/climber's-right side on moderate 20-40° snow, working around a bergschrund near 7,900 ft, usually passable on its left side.

climbing_route.label: Summit snowfield and arête
climbing_route.notes: The final summit snowfield steepens from ~30-40° to nearly 50° near the top — firm enough for front-pointing but not always secure for flat-footing — with snow flukes commonly used for running belays before a short snow arête leads to the summit rocks.

climbing_route.label: Rock rib above Lake of the Angels
climbing_route.notes: From Lake of the Angels the route leaves any trail and goes cross-country: climb roughly 800 ft up onto a rock rib above the lake's basin and cross to its north side. The gully/rib terrain above the lake is loose and route-finding is nontrivial in cloud or fresh snow; snow typically lingers on the north-facing basin above the lake well into summer, so an ice axe (and sometimes microspikes/crampons) is worth carrying into early-mid summer. Water is scarce above the lake.

climbing_route.label: Notch on the west ridge below St. Peter's Gate
climbing_route.notes: Follow the terrain up toward a notch on Mount Stone's west ridge below the feature known as St. Peter's Gate.

climbing_route.label: Talus/boulder terrain to the summit block
climbing_route.notes: Continue through talus/boulder terrain toward the summit block; the 6,618 ft high point.

climbing_route.label: LeConte Glacier contour from Sentinel Pass
climbing_route.notes: Old Guard Peak is climbed from Sentinel Pass: contour onto the LeConte Glacier. Committing, remote glacier terrain — carry a full topo map and glacier gear; there is no easy bail once past Cache Col.

climbing_route.label: Southwest snow couloir/snowfinger
climbing_route.notes: Ascend a moderate, gradually-angled snow couloir/snowfinger on the peak's southwest side to gain the summit ridge; watch for a bergschrund/moat late season.

climbing_route.label: Summit ridge
climbing_route.notes: Finish on short scrambling on solid, high-friction gabbro to the true summit (8,240-8,260 ft).
